variants.name: Typed broker TTL publish (amqplib)
variants.implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits Node's runtime, so the broker route is the same amqplib call - typed as Options.Publish - with the expiration field constrained at compile time to the string of milliseconds the wire expects, which removes the classic NaN/undefined bug class where the broker sees no TTL. The message contract lives in the types: an Expiring<T> envelope with an absolute expiresAt is what the consumer re-checks, while the broker enforces the same limit per message or per queue. Choose this whenever messages outlive the process; the type layer adds no enforcement of its own.
pitfalls: A branded EpochMillis keeps unit errors out but not clock errors: nothing in the type stops a caller using a local time or seconds value, so construct the value in one helper that reads Date.now() once.
Types are erased at runtime - an incoming message is still unknown JSON, so the expiresAt field must be validated (or parsed into the envelope) before it is trusted.
tsconfig target/lib affects whether AbortSignal.timeout, structuredClone or newer timer types are visible; a missing lib entry surfaces as a compile error rather than a runtime check.

variants.name: Typed deadline envelope plus AbortSignal.timeout
variants.idiom_name: Expiring<T> envelope with branded EpochMillis and AbortSignal.timeout
variants.implementation_notes: For in-process work the TypeScript-specific contribution is the contract, not the mechanism: an Expiring<T> envelope whose expiresAt is a branded EpochMillis makes the deadline part of every message type and a single isStale() helper the only sanctioned comparison, while AbortSignal.timeout(ms) (or a setTimeout with Timeout.unref) supplies the runtime deadline. That replaces the classic per-message expiry manager with a value plus one primitive, and the compiler keeps producers from forgetting to stamp it. It remains best-effort inside one process, so broker TTL is still the answer once messages cross it.
pitfalls: The branded type stops accidental unit mixes only if it is still a number at runtime; a cast from user input ('as EpochMillis') launders any value, so validate at the boundary.
AbortSignal.timeout cannot be cancelled: finishing work early does not clear the timer, and listeners attached to the signal keep the payload alive until it fires - remove them explicitly.
deadline arithmetic on branded numbers still yields plain numbers; re-branding at each hop is what prevents seconds and milliseconds from silently meeting in the same expression.
